title: The Edict of Milan (313)
hookLine: Christianity becomes legal, and the persecuted become the favored

lines: A NOTICE ON A WALL IN NICOMEDIA.
cards: A notice goes up on a public wall in Nicomedia, a great city of the eastern empire.
It's a letter from two emperors who have met at Milan and agreed on how the empire will treat religion: Constantine, who ruled the west, and Licinius, who was taking hold of the east.

The writer Lactantius copied it out in full, and noted where it was posted: the same city where, by his account, an order to tear down churches and burn scriptures had been nailed up some years before.
Same city, opposite message. People who had hidden their books, buried their friends and kept their heads down could walk past and read it.

teach.b: In paraphrase, the emperors grant to Christians, and to all others, the free power to follow whatever religion each person chooses. Not Christians instead of everyone else: Christians and everyone else.
The reason sounds very Roman: so that whatever divine power there is in heaven may be kindly toward us and toward all who live under our rule. Then it gets practical.
Meeting places and property taken from Christians are to be handed back at once, without payment, and anyone who bought one in good faith can ask the state for compensation.
Freedom isn't only a sentence; it's a key returned to a door. Now the name.

teach.h: AN EDICT THAT REACHES US AS A LETTER.
teach.b: What we call the Edict of Milan reaches us as a letter, the copy Licinius had posted in Nicomedia. The name stuck anyway.
Then the turn: the persecuted become the favored. Eusebius keeps letters from the months that follow in which Constantine sends money to clergy in Africa and frees clergy from public duties.
The first letter to Timothy had asked prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life." Here was that quiet life, arriving all at once.
And for good and ill: the letter's words were freedom for all. Some readers point out that later, when Christians held power, that promise didn't always hold for others. The long story has both.

how: Some churches pray in their services for those in authority and for people who suffer for their faith, and some Christian groups work for religious freedom for people of every faith.

practice: Bring to mind one person near you whose faith is different from yours, or who has none, and picture them on an ordinary day keeping what they keep: a prayer, a fast, a holiday, a quiet Sunday morning with no church in it.
Don't argue with it; just let them be free in the picture. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, simply wish them well, as they are.

wordCard.voice: Constantine. One of the two emperors whose agreement at Milan gave Christians, and all others, freedom to follow their own religion, and handed back what had been taken.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom for all. Christians, and all others, in one breath. That's day seven hundred sixty-seven.
